344.title: Lamp of beauty
344.hook: the Jaap moves into Persian: He is the glorious one, the lamp of beauty (Jaap)
344.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Jaap Sahib move through its Persian and Arabic passages each morning in the same rhythm as the rest, and the words husn (beauty) and charaag (lamp) are still familiar in Punjabi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naad, the sound within sounds, and your line, the dance of dances. Today, Jaap changes language in the middle of the hymn.

A friend who speaks three languages is telling you a story in English. Then they reach the part they really care about, and suddenly it's Spanish, or Punjabi, or Tagalog. Some things only sound right in one language: grandma's words, the word for that kind of evening. Partway through Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru does something like that. He moves into Persian, the language of poets and courts, and starts talking about beauty.
screen: `A FRIEND SWITCHES LANGUAGES.` → `SOME THINGS SOUND RIGHT IN ONE.` → `JAAP SWITCHES INTO PERSIAN.`

segments.voice: In the Tenth Guru's world, Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government papers, and of a great tradition of love poetry. The Guru knew it well; his letter to the emperor, the Zafarnama, is written in it. So when Jaap moves into Persian and Arabic words, it isn't showing off. It reaches for a language with a long habit of praising beauty. The lines begin with a little word, ki, meaning something like: for You are. One of them says the One is husnal charaag. Husn is beauty, the same word Punjabi still uses for a lovely face or a lovely view. Charaag, or chiragh, is a small oil lamp of the kind that lit houses and shrines. The lamp of beauty. A lamp isn't beautiful because of its own shape; it's beautiful because it lets you see everything else. Lamplight makes a room golden. So the line suggests that beauty itself has a source, and that every lovely thing is lit by it. In the same Persian stretch, Jaap uses names like kareem, generous, and raheem, merciful, names Muslims also use for God. The Tenth Guru brings them into Sikh morning prayer without hesitating. Jaap reaches for every language the Guru had, Braj, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, as if to say: no single tongue holds the One, and every tongue can praise.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF COURTS AND POETS.` · `HUSN: BEAUTY. CHARAAG: A LAMP.` · `A LAMP LETS YOU SEE EVERYTHING ELSE.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM: SHARED NAMES.` · then, large: `LAMP OF BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Find one beautiful thing near you, the grain in a table, light on a wall, the curve of a mug handle, someone's handwriting, and rest your eyes on it. Then notice the light that's letting you see it, a window, a lamp, a screen's glow, and breathe slowly with the two together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the word of wonder.
Husnal charaag. Husn is beauty; charaag, a lamp — the One as the lamp that lets every lovely thing be seen.
Your line: makes a room golden. The lamp is what lets the beauty show. Day three hundred forty-four.

345.title: The provider
345.hook: in Persian again: He is the one who gives daily bread (Jaap)
345.howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to earn honestly (kirat karni), remember the Name (naam japna) and share (vand chhakna), and every gurdwara runs a langar, a free kitchen open to everyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, husnal charaag, the lamp of beauty, and your line, makes a room golden. Today the Persian lines keep going, and come down to the kitchen table.

Pick up a slice of bread and count the hands. Someone plowed a field and planted the wheat, then watched the sky all summer hoping for rain. A harvester driver, a miller, a trucker on a night highway, a baker up at four, a cashier, whoever carried the bag home. One slice, and dozens of people you'll never meet. Behind them, the rain and the sun and the soil, which nobody made. Every meal is a long chain of giving, and Jaap Sahib names the start of it.
screen: `ONE SLICE OF BREAD.` → `DOZENS OF HANDS.` → `A LONG CHAIN OF GIVING.`

segments.voice: In its Persian lines, Jaap says the One is rozi dihind, the giver of daily bread, and raazak, the provider. Rozi comes from roz, a day: the day's portion, the food, the wages, the livelihood that keeps a household going until tomorrow. Punjabi still says rozi roti for earning a living, the daily bread and the daily flatbread. Raazak is an Arabic word for the One who provides for every creature. So in the middle of all the cosmic praise, timeless, formless, sun of suns, Jaap stops at something as plain as lunch. That's very Sikh. Guru Nanak, in Japji, says there is one Giver for all living beings, and asks never to forget that One. But notice the Sikh balance. Trusting the Provider has never meant sitting and waiting. The three pillars Sikhs are taught are naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing what you have. You earn your bread honestly, thank the Giver for it, and share it. That's why every gurdwara has a langar, a free kitchen where anyone can eat. The bread passes through Sikh hands and goes straight back out to whoever walks in the door. In Sikh practice, the chain of giving doesn't end at your plate; it runs through it.

segments.voice: Hold something you're about to eat, or think of the last thing you ate, and trace it back one pair of hands at a time: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, who grew it, thanking each one silently. Then go one step further, to the rain, the sun and the soil, and rest there with your breath. If you pray, you can thank the Giver of daily bread.

346.title: Gobind, Mukand
346.hook: gobinde mukande udaare apaare: the Sustainer, the Liberator, generous, infinite (Jaap)
346.howItsDone: In gurdwaras and homes, the line gobinde mukande udaare apaare is often recited or sung together, and Gobind is one of many names for the Divine Sikhs use in prayer and kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the provider, giver of rozi, and your line, daily bread. Today, a line with a familiar name in it.

Gobinde. Mukande. Udaare. Apaare. Four words, each ending in the same open sound, like four drumbeats. Said fast, in a room reciting Jaap, the line is easy to catch even without knowing the language. And one of those four words is a name you've heard many times this year, the name of a man. It's a little like finding your teacher's name written into the song he taught you.
screen: `GOBINDE, MUKANDE, UDAARE, APAARE.` → `FOUR WORDS LIKE FOUR DRUMBEATS.` → `A NAME YOU ALREADY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Take the words one at a time. Gobind is a very old Indian name for the Divine, often explained as the sustainer, the one who cares for the earth and all that lives on it. It appears again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, long before the Tenth Guru was born. Mukand: the liberator, the one who gives mukti, freedom from everything that binds. Udaar: generous, open-handed; Punjabi still uses it for a big-hearted person. And apaar: paar is the far shore of a river, and apaar has no far shore. Infinite. Sustainer, Liberator, Generous, Without end. Now the name. The Tenth Guru was born Gobind Rai, and tradition says that at the founding of the Khalsa he became Gobind Singh. So when he writes gobinde in his own hymn, his name is right there in the praise. Sikhs don't hear that as the Guru praising himself. The Guru was clear that he was a servant of the One, and his name, like so many Indian names, was taken from a name of God. A child named for the Sustainer grows up to sing the Sustainer's praise. Then look at the pairing: udaar and apaar, generous and infinite, side by side. Something infinite that kept to itself would be grand and far away. Something generous with limits would run out. Jaap praises the One who is both: giving, and never running out.

347.title: One form, many sights
347.hook: ek moorat anek darsan: one form seen in countless ways (Jaap, roaaval)
347.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this roaal stanza of Jaap Sahib each morning, and the idea of the world as the One's khel, play, runs through Sikh scripture and kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gobind, the Sustainer, and your line, generous and infinite. Today Jaap slows into longer lines, and plays with one and many.

Bedtime, and a parent is reading a story out loud. The dragon gets a deep growl, the princess a bright, quick voice, and the old king, the narrator and the talking cat each sound different. The child in bed believes every one of them. Nothing came from outside: all those voices were in one person the whole time. Then the book closes, the light goes off, and there's just one voice again, saying goodnight. Many from one, and back to one. Jaap Sahib has a stanza that works like that.
screen: `ONE READER, MANY VOICES.` → `A DRAGON, A PRINCESS, A TALKING CAT.` → `THE BOOK CLOSES: ONE VOICE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: In a meter called roaal, with longer, rolling lines, one stanza opens: ek moorat anek darsan, keen roop anek. Ek is one. Moorat is form or likeness. Anek is many, countless. Darsan is a sight, a glimpse, the word Sikhs use for seeing something holy, as when people go for darshan at the Golden Temple. One form, countless sights; You made forms beyond number. Then: khel khel akhel khelan, ant ko phir ek. Khel is play, a game. Having played the play, beyond all play, at the end, again One. Earlier, Jaap called the One aroop, formless. Now it says the One shows itself in countless forms. Sikh readers don't hear a contradiction. Think of the reader at bedtime: no dragon's growl of their own, and yet every voice in the story is theirs. Sikh scripture often calls the world the One's khel, the great unfolding game: in that reading, every person, every animal, every grain of sand is one more voice in the same story. And then the book closes, and it all folds back. Again, One. That reading can change how people look at each other. The rude driver, your sister, the stranger on the bus, the friend you think you know completely: each a different voice from the same source, and none of them the whole picture of anyone.

segments.voice: Picture someone you know well, then see them from angles you usually don't: as a small child, as their parents see them, at three in the morning, on their best day. Let each picture be one more voice in their story, then let them fold back into the one person. If you pray, you can say ek moorat anek darsan softly.

348.title: Ender and sustainer of all
348.hook: sarab kaal hain, sarab paal hain: He ends all and He sustains all (Jaap)
348.howItsDone: Sikhs understand births, deaths and every change as happening within hukam, the One's order, and recite Jaap's pairing of the One who ends and keeps all things each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one form, seen in countless ways, and your line, one, seen many ways. Today, two words that sound like opposites, held by one hand.

Walk through a forest in late autumn. The leaves are coming down, thousands of them, every one a small ending. Kick through them, and underneath is dark, crumbly soil: last year's leaves, already turning into food for the tree that dropped them. The same tree is letting go and being fed, at once, by the same falling. A gardener knows this. So does anyone who has sat in a hospital where one family grieves down the hall from another holding a newborn. Endings and keepings sit close together, and Jaap Sahib puts them in one breath.
screen: `AUTUMN LEAVES COMING DOWN.` → `LAST YEAR'S LEAVES FEED THE TREE.` → `ENDINGS AND KEEPINGS, CLOSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The words are sarab kaal and sarab paal. Sarab means all. Kaal you met eleven days ago: time, and death, the thing that ends. Paal is the root of paalna, the Punjabi word for raising a child: feeding, protecting, keeping alive. So Jaap salutes the One as the ending of all things and the keeping of all things. Now set this beside the glide's first word. On day three hundred thirty-seven, Jaap bowed to akaal, the One without kaal. Here the same One is called the kaal of everything. A contradiction? Not as Sikh scripture reads it. In Sikh teaching, the One isn't subject to time, but every ending in time happens within the One's order, which Sikhs call hukam. Guru Nanak's Japji says everything is within hukam, and nothing is outside it: births, deaths, harvests, partings. The Tenth Guru is willing to use the hard name too. Elsewhere in his writing he speaks of the One as Kaal and Mahakaal, great Time, the power that brings all things to their close. He doesn't pretend endings aren't real, or that they come from somewhere else. But here Jaap doesn't say sarab kaal alone; it comes with sarab paal. The hand that ends is the hand that keeps, as the leaf falls and the soil feeds the tree. For Sikhs living through an ending, that pairing can be a quiet comfort: in Jaap, the One who closes doors is also the One who keeps.

segments.voice: Think back over this week and find one thing that ended, a project, a season, a habit, a conversation, and hold it gently for a breath. Then find one thing that began, even something small, and hold that too, letting the two sit side by side without choosing between them. If you pray, you can place both in the same hand.

349.title: House of compassion
349.hook: karunaalay hain: He is the home of compassion (Jaap, harbolmana)
349.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the quick harbolmana lines of Jaap Sahib each morning, and daya, compassion, is taught as one of the core virtues alongside truth, contentment, humility and love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sarab kaal, sarab paal, and your line, ends and keeps. Today, a new quick meter, and a house.

Some people have one kitchen like this: a grandmother's, an aunt's, a friend's mom's. You could show up unannounced, any hour, after any kind of day, and the kettle went on before you'd finished saying hello. Nobody asked what you'd done wrong. Nobody made you earn the chair. You came in, and you were cared for, because that's what the house was for. Some people are kind now and then. Some people are a place you can go. Jaap Sahib names the One like that second kind.
screen: `ONE KITCHEN YOU COULD ALWAYS GO TO.` → `THE KETTLE WENT ON BEFORE HELLO.` → `SOME PEOPLE ARE A PLACE.`

segments.voice: Jaap shifts into another meter, harbolmana, with tiny, fast lines of two words each, and the first is karunaalay hain. Two words fused. Karunaa is compassion, the feeling that moves toward someone's suffering. Aalay, from aalaya, is a dwelling, a home. It hides in the name of a mountain range: Himalaya is hima, snow, plus aalaya, home. So karunaalay is the home of compassion. You are the house where compassion lives. That's different from compassionate. A compassionate person feels it sometimes, on a good day. A home of compassion is where it lives all the time, whether anyone visits or not: the kitchen where the kettle is always ready. Sikhs have a word close to karunaa for a human virtue: daya, kindness, mercy, often listed among the virtues a Sikh tries to grow, with truth, contentment, humility and love. And Guru Nanak gives daya a startling job. In Japji, he takes the old myth of a bull holding the earth on its back and says: the bull is dharma, righteousness, and dharma is the child of daya, of compassion. Compassion is what holds the world up. So when Jaap calls the One the house of compassion, it also hints at what a Sikh home and a Sikh heart might try to be. Not kind sometimes. A place people can come.

350.title: Breaker of the cruel
350.hook: khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain: He breaks the cruel and adorns the earth (Jaap, harbolmana)
350.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the harbolmana lines, karunaalay hain, khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain, briskly each morning in Jaap Sahib, and the saint-soldier ideal joins compassion with standing up to cruelty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karunaa, and your line, home of compassion. Today the same quick stanza keeps going, and it gets fierce.

Anyone who has kept a garden knows the two jobs. One is planting: seeds, bulbs, the hopeful part. The other is pulling. Bindweed wrapping around the beans. A vine strangling the rosebush. Pull them, and the garden breathes again; skip it, and no amount of planting will save it. A good gardener is gentle and ruthless at once, and nobody calls that a contradiction. It's what loving a garden looks like. Jaap Sahib puts both jobs into a single rhyme.
screen: `A GARDEN HAS TWO JOBS.` → `PLANTING, AND PULLING.` → `GENTLE AND RUTHLESS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Right after karunaalay, the home of compassion, the harbolmana lines go on: khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain. Khal is the cruel one, the wicked, the person who preys on others; Punjabi still uses it for a scoundrel. Khanddan is breaking, shattering. Mahi is the earth, and manddan is adorning, making beautiful. The two halves rhyme, khanddan, manddan, and the rhyme is the teaching. Breaking the cruel and adorning the earth aren't two jobs. They're one, like pulling the bindweed so the roses can bloom. And the line sits directly after compassion; Jaap doesn't separate them. In the Tenth Guru's world, compassion that never stood up to cruelty would be a kitchen with the door open to thieves. The ideal of the saint-soldier, gentle in the heart and ready in the hands, is in these tiny lines. The breaking is never the point on its own. Cruelty gets broken so that the earth can be adorned: fed, sheltered, made fair. And the week ends here. Six days ago, Jaap switched into Persian and called the One the lamp of beauty. Then the provider, giver of daily bread. Gobind, generous and infinite. One form, seen in countless ways. The ender and sustainer of all. The house of compassion. And today, the breaker of the cruel, who adorns the earth.
screen: `KHAL KHANDDAN: BREAKING THE CRUEL.` · `MAHI MANDDAN: ADORNING THE EARTH.` · `ONE JOB, LIKE WEEDING A GARDEN.` · `RIGHT AFTER COMPASSION.` · then, large: `BREAK CRUELTY, ADORN EARTH.`

segments.voice: Think about the day ahead and where a little cruelty might show up: a joke at someone's expense, gossip, a sharp tone with someone who can't answer back, your own inner voice being harsh with you. Picture yourself not joining in, or gently changing the subject, and then picture one thing you could make a little more beautiful instead. Breathe.
Khal khanddan. The cruel one, broken — paired with mahi manddan, the earth adorned: the One who shatters cruelty and beautifies the world, in a single rhyme.
Your line: break cruelty, adorn earth. Planting and pulling are one job. Day three hundred fifty: a week, done.
